First, let's make a diagram of the situation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14196324/assets/7595abcc3939c90d84bdcf93e7a773386b6392ea24a48cc0d4daeb9a2e579b65.png)

Let $x$ and $y$ be the width and height of the rectangle, respectively. Given a width $x,$ the height $y$ of the rectangle rises up to the curve $y=35-5{x}^{6}.$

We want to maximize the area of the rectangle, which is given by

$$
A=xy=x(35-5{x}^{6})=35x-5{x}^{7}.
$$

Let's compute the critical points. Taking the derivative of the area, we get

$$
{A}^{′}(x)=35-35{x}^{6},
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 35-35{x}^{6} & =0 \\ 35{x}^{6} & =35 \\ {x}^{6} & =1 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $x=1$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(x).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\sqrt[6]{7})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $0.5$ | $$ | $1.2$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $x=1$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting rectangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest area ${A}_{\text{max}}$ that a rectangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{\text{max}}=A(1) & =35(1)-5(1)^{7} \\  & =35-5 \\  & =30.\end{aligned}
$$
